title: Single-arm meta-analysis
text: Use this module when there is no comparison: you want the pooled prevalence of a condition, the complication rate of a procedure, or the average value of a measure in a population. Follow the three-step flow, with a much shorter step 2, because without a control group several fields stop making sense.

title: Single-arm meta-analysis
text:
Step 1, the data
Two submodules, chosen on the previous page.
Single proportions



Column
What it is




study
the study label


event
number of participants with the outcome


n
sample size of the arm



Single means



Column
What it is




study
the study label


n
sample size


mean
mean value of the outcome


sd
standard deviation of the outcome




A study reporting a median is accepted too



Column
What it is




study, n
as above


median, q1, q3
median and quartiles of the outcome



min and max are optional. They can stand in for the quartiles when a paper reports only a range, and the conversion is then less precise.
A median with sd and nothing else is refused, and on purpose. A median cannot be turned into a mean without the quartiles or the range, and meta does not complain about it: it drops the study from the pooling with no message. Better to hear it here than to publish a review missing studies you never knew were excluded.


The two can be mixed in one file
Fill the columns each study reports and leave the rest empty. The example dataset does exactly that: eight studies with mean and SD, four with median and quartiles. MetaVidence converts the median studies before pooling, using the method of Luo and colleagues for the mean and that of Shi and colleagues for the standard deviation, which are the current defaults of the meta package.
The Data check reports how many studies were converted, so the number is in front of you before anything runs and can go straight into the methods section.
Mean and SD are the values the study measured directly. The conversion estimates them from the median and quartiles, so that a study reporting a median can join the analysis.
Extra columns stay available for subgroup analysis and meta-regression, as in the other modules. The Data check verifies the required ones, counts the studies and flags problems, including event larger than n.

title: Single-arm meta-analysis
text:
Step 2, the parameters
The outcome direction field and the group name fields do not exist here: with no comparison, there is no “favors experimental” or “favors control” to label.

Single proportions
Outcome name goes into titles and file names, as always.
Summary measure (sm) (default PLOGIT) chooses the scale on which the proportions are pooled. Proportions near 0% or 100% have a very small variance on the raw scale, which is what the transformations address:

PLOGIT, logit. The default.
PFT, Freeman-Tukey double arcsine. Stabilizes the variance at proportions close to the extremes. The back-transformation to the percentage scale depends on the study sample sizes.
PAS, plain arcsine.
PLN, log of the proportion.
PRAW, raw proportion, untransformed.

Results always return to the percentage scale in plots and tables, so the transformation is a choice of method, not of presentation.
Method (default Inverse) chooses between Inverse, inverse variance, and GLMM, a random-intercept logistic model.
Inverse applies inverse-variance weighting to the transformed proportions. With studies that have zero events, or proportions very close to 0% or 100%, it adds 0.5 to each cell as a continuity correction. GLMM models the counts directly and applies no such correction. GLMM is normally paired with Tau method at ML, and Inverse with REML.






GLMM has no weight column



A GLMM fit produces no per-study weight, so the forest plot comes out without the Weight column and with every square the same size. This is not a defect of the plot: the weight simply does not exist in that model. The Inverse method does produce per-study weights, so the column is present there.








GLMM requires PLOGIT



If you switch sm to PFT, PAS, PLN or PRAW and leave the method at GLMM, the analysis stops with an error message. When you change sm, set the method back to Inverse.


Analysis model and Tau method work as in the binary module.
This submodule has no Prediction interval, no Random CI method and no Prediction method.


Single means
Summary measure (sm) (default MRAW) has two options. MRAW pools the mean in the original measurement unit. MLN pools the mean on the log scale, which requires strictly positive values.
Analysis model, Tau method (default REML) and Prediction interval (default Yes) work as in the binary module. There is no Method field, no Random CI method and no Prediction method.

title: Single-arm meta-analysis
text:
Step 3, export and results
Both submodules carry the same cards as the paired modules: Forest plot, Leave-one-out analysis, Funnel plot, Small-study effects with Egger’s test, Subgroup analysis, Meta-regression and the two summary tables as XLSX.

title: Network meta-analysis
text:
Use this module when you have several treatments and not all of them were compared directly. The network uses the direct comparisons to estimate the indirect ones: if A was compared with B, and B with C, then A against C can be estimated.
Follow the three-step flow, but both the input and the output are different here.

title: Network meta-analysis
text:
Step 1, the data
The format is long, one row per arm rather than per study. There are no .e and .c columns: studies repeat, once for each arm.



study
treatment
responders
sampleSize




Study A
Drug A
12
120


Study A
Drug B
20
118


Study B
Drug A
15
130


Study B
Placebo
23
128



There are three submodules:



Submodule
Required columns




Binary
study, treatment, responders, sampleSize


Continuous
study, treatment, mean, std.dev, sampleSize


Pre-calculated
study, treat1, treat2, TE, lower, upper



In the pre-calculated submodule a row is a comparison, not an arm, which is why treat1 and treat2 exist.






The treatment name must match exactly



Drug A, drug A and Drug-A become three different nodes in the network. It is the most common error here, and the network comes out disconnected with nothing pointing at the reason. Standardize the names in the spreadsheet before loading.


Each study needs at least two arms. Studies with three or more are accepted, and the Data check reports how many there are, because they require special statistical handling, which netmeta already does.

title: Network meta-analysis
text:
Step 2, the parameters

Outcome settings
Outcome name goes into titles and file names.
Summary measure (sm) depends on the submodule: RR, OR and RD in the binary one, MD and SMD in the continuous one, and HR, RR, OR, MD, SMD in the pre-calculated one. Each behaves as in the paired modules.
Reference treatment (optional) sets which treatment the others are compared against in the forest plot. Left blank, the app picks one on its own. This does not change the network, only the point of view of the figure.
For ranking, smaller values are (default Good) tells the app whether smaller values are good or bad. It sets the direction of the P-score ranking. For an outcome such as mortality, where smaller values are desirable, choose Good; for one such as treatment response, where larger values are desirable, choose Bad.






This field flips the whole ranking



Getting it wrong raises no error and no warning. The P-score comes out computed, neat, and in reverse order. Check it before reporting any ranking.




Statistical settings (advanced)
Analysis model (default Random-effects) and Tau method (default REML) work as in the binary module. In a network the random-effects model is almost always the right choice, because the network gathers studies that are even more diverse than in a pairwise comparison.
There is no Prediction interval, Random CI method or Prediction method in this module.

title: Network meta-analysis
text:
Step 3, export and results
This is the part that differs most from the other modules. There are eight cards.
Forest plot compares every treatment against the chosen reference.
Network graph draws the network: treatments are the nodes and direct comparisons are the edges, with thickness proportional to the amount of direct evidence. It is worth being the first thing you look at, because it shows at once whether the network is connected and where the evidence is thin.
League table puts every pairwise comparison into a single table, exported to Excel. It is the table that usually goes into supplementary material.
Between-study heterogeneity opens the design-based decomposition and the Q statistics, which separate heterogeneity within designs from inconsistency between them.
Node splitting compares direct and indirect evidence for each comparison where both exist. It is the local test of inconsistency.
P-score ranking orders the treatments. The P-score runs from 0 to 1 and summarizes how likely a treatment is to be better than the others.
Comparison-adjusted funnel plot examines small-study effects across the network comparisons.
Pairwise object downloads the pairwise object used to build the network, useful for checking and reproducibility.

title: MetaVidence tutorials
text: MetaVidence does meta-analysis without code. You load a spreadsheet, choose the parameters and get publication-ready plots and tables, all in the browser, with nothing to install and without your data leaving your computer.

title: MetaVidence tutorials
text:
Where to start

Get started shows how to open MetaVidence in the browser, and how to install R, RStudio and the package if you would rather run it on your own computer.
The three-step flow walks the screens end to end: data, parameters and export. Every module works this way.
Your module’s page covers only what changes in it, such as the required columns and the summary measure.

Every module ships an example dataset with 12 studies. It is worth running the analysis on it before using your own data, so you can see what each screen produces without preparing a spreadsheet.

title: MetaVidence tutorials
text:
Choosing the module



You have…
Use




Event counts and sample sizes in both groups
Binary outcomes


Mean and SD, median and IQR, or a mix of the two
Continuous outcomes


The effect already calculated, with CI or standard error
Pre-calculated effects


One proportion or mean per study, no comparison
Single arm


Three or more treatments compared indirectly
Network meta-analysis


2×2 diagnostic accuracy tables
Diagnostic meta-analysis



Have more than one outcome to analyse? Once you have picked the module, follow Multiple outcomes at once to run them all in a single pass.

title: MetaVidence tutorials
text:
How to cite
If MetaVidence produced results you are publishing, cite MetaVidence and the analysis packages. Citations are what keep this free academic tool alive and maintained, and recording which software produced your numbers is part of a reproducible analysis.

title: Get started
text: There are two ways to use MetaVidence, and both do exactly the same maths. Start with the browser, which asks you to install nothing. If you are going to use it often, the R route is worth it: it opens much faster and works without an internet connection.

title: Get started
text:
1. Open the site
Go to metavidence.com. No account to create, nothing to install, no file sent to any server.

title: Get started
text:
2. Wait for the first load
On the first visit you get a screen with the word Loading and a bar. The browser is downloading R and the statistical packages compiled to run inside it. That takes a few minutes on an ordinary connection.
While you wait, you can use the two links on that screen. They open in another tab and do not interrupt the loading.
From the second visit on, the browser already has the files stored and starts much faster.

title: Get started
text:
3. Follow the flow
With the app open, follow the three-step flow: it shows how to pick the module, load the data, set the parameters and export the results.

title: Get started
text:
1. Install R
R is the language that does the maths. RStudio on its own does nothing without it, which is why R comes first.

Go to cran.r-project.org.
Click the link for your system: Download R for Windows, Download R for macOS or Download R for Linux.
On Windows, click base and then Download R for Windows. On macOS, pick the .pkg file that matches your processor: the arm64 one for Macs with an Apple chip (M1 onwards) and the other one for Intel Macs.
Open the downloaded file and follow the installer, accepting the defaults.

MetaVidence needs R 4.1 or newer. Any version downloaded from CRAN today qualifies.

title: Get started
text:
2. Install RStudio
RStudio is the window through which you use R. You can live without it, but it makes everything simpler.

Go to posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop.
Download the free version, RStudio Desktop, for your system.
Open the file and follow the installer.

title: Get started
section: 3. Open RStudio and find the Console
text:
3. Open RStudio and find the Console
Open RStudio. The window is split into panes; the one that matters now is the Console, usually at the bottom left, with a blinking >.
That is where you paste the commands in the next steps. Paste the line and press Enter.

title: Get started
text:
4. Install the package
MetaVidence has been submitted to CRAN. Until it is accepted, install it from the source repository. Paste these two lines into the Console, one at a time, pressing Enter after each:
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ValbertOCF/MetaVidence", subdir = "pkg")
The first line installs the helper that can install from GitHub. The second downloads MetaVidence and the packages it depends on, among them meta, metafor, netmeta, mada and shiny. That is a lot of files, so the first installation takes a few minutes. Let it run until the > comes back on its own in the Console.
Once MetaVidence is on CRAN, this becomes a single line, install.packages("metavidence"), and this page will say so.
If R asks something like “Do you want to install from sources the package which needs compilation?”, answer no and press Enter. The prebuilt version is enough and installs far faster.

title: Get started
text:
5. Run MetaVidence
Once the installation finishes, paste:
metavidence::run_app()
MetaVidence opens in an RStudio window or in your browser, looking exactly like the online version. From here on it is the same three-step flow.






The Console stays busy while the app runs



That is normal: R is serving the application. To get the Console back, close the MetaVidence window or click the stop symbol (the red square) in the corner of the Console.

title: Get started
text:
6. Next times
You install only once. After that, open RStudio and run just:
metavidence::run_app()
To update when a new version comes out, repeat the command from step 4.

title: Get started
text:
If something goes wrong
The install command returns an error saying the package is not available. Check that the line was pasted whole, including the quotes. If it is correct, your R may be too old: run R.version.string in the Console and confirm it is 4.1 or higher.
The installation stops partway, on one of the packages MetaVidence depends on. Run install.packages("package_name") for that package alone, read its error message, then repeat the command from step 4.
run_app() says it could not find the application directory. Install again with the command from step 4.
Nothing opens when you run run_app(). Force the browser with:
metavidence::run_app(launch.browser = TRUE)

title: Diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis
text: Use this module when each study gives a 2x2 accuracy table: true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives. Follow the three-step flow, but step 2 is much shorter and step 3 is the most different of all the modules.

title: Diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis
text:
Step 1, the data



Column
What it is




study
the study label


TP
true positives


FP
false positives


FN
false negatives


TN
true negatives



In the comparative module there is one more column, test, with the name of the test, and each study appears twice, one row per test.
Extra columns, such as Region, stay available for subgroup analysis. The Data check verifies the required ones, counts the studies and flags negative or blank cells.

title: Diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis
text:
Why this module is different
In diagnostic meta-analysis the outcome is bivariate: sensitivity and specificity move together and are correlated. A more sensitive test is usually less specific, because the threshold moves. That is why the model is the bivariate binomial GLMM, and not two separate models. That is the model the Cochrane Handbook for DTA Reviews v2.0 specifies in chapter 10.
This has a practical consequence: looking at pooled sensitivity alone gets you nowhere. The main result is the operating point, sensitivity and specificity together, with their confidence intervals.

title: Diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis
text:
Step 2, the parameters
This is the shortest step 2 in MetaVidence, because most of the choices in a bivariate model are not configurable field by field.

Single test module
Outcome name goes into titles and file names.
Analysis model (default Random-effects) affects the sensitivity, specificity and diagnostic odds ratio forest plots.






The bivariate model ignores this field



The Reitsma bivariate model is always random-effects, by construction. Switching to Fixed-effect changes the forest plots, but neither the summary point nor the summary operating point.


There is no sm, Method, Tau method, prediction interval or group name here: none of those fields applies to the bivariate model.


Comparative module
Besides Outcome name, there are Test A and Test B, which fill themselves with the names found in the test column. They define which test is compared against which, and the order the two appear in the figures.

title: Diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis
text:
Step 3, export and results

Single test
Sensitivity forest plot and Specificity forest plot, one for each, with sensitivity computed as TP / (TP + FN) and specificity as TN / (TN + FP).
Summary point, with the studies, the pooled sensitivity and specificity, a 95% confidence region and a 95% prediction region. There is no curve and no AUC: those belong to the HSROC model, which the handbook notes cannot be fitted in R with lme4. The bivariate model estimates a point, so a point is what the plot shows.






The forest plots show studies, not a pooled estimate



The forests deliberately carry no pooled diamond. Averaging sensitivity and specificity separately ignores the correlation between them, which is what section 10.2.3 of the handbook rules out. Every pooled number in this module comes from the bivariate fit, and there is only one of each.


Diagnostic odds ratio, with its own forest plot. The DOR summarizes accuracy in a single number, combining sensitivity and specificity. It is useful for comparing tests, but it says nothing about where the balance between the two errors lies, so it does not replace the sensitivity and specificity pair.
Threshold effect, the correlation between sensitivity and the false-positive rate across studies, with the Deeks test for small-study effects. A positive correlation suggests the studies used different positivity thresholds, which is the confounder specific to diagnostic accuracy.






There is no subgroup analysis here



To the bivariate model a subgroup and a head-to-head test comparison are the same thing: a covariate. The handbook says so plainly, calling them both “group”. That model lives in the comparative workflow, so splitting one test by a column belongs there rather than being duplicated as a weaker version here.
The app warns when there are fewer than 4 studies: the bivariate model estimates 5 parameters and converges anyway, but the estimate becomes unstable. Converging is not the same as being trustworthy.




Comparative
Sensitivity by test and Specificity by test, the forest plots split by test.
Comparative summary points, both tests on the same plot, each with its own confidence region. Both come from one joint model, grouped by study, so a paired design keeps its pairing.
Overall comparison, Sensitivity comparison and Specificity comparison: three likelihood-ratio tests, one for overall accuracy and one for each component. Having the overall test significant and the two specific ones not significant is common and informative: the tests differ in the balance between the two errors, not in either one alone.






The comparative module requires paired studies



Each study must have assessed both tests in the same population. Studies with only one of the tests stay out of the joint comparison. Comparing tests assessed in different populations means comparing populations, not tests.

title: Binary outcomes
text:
Use this module when each study reports how many events occurred in each group and the size of each group. That covers yes or no outcomes: mortality, recurrence, response to treatment.
If your effect already comes calculated from the paper, the right module is pre-calculated effects, not this one.
This page covers what belongs to this module. The screens and the buttons are in the three-step flow.

title: Binary outcomes
text:
Step 1, the data
Five required columns, with these exact names:



Column
What it is




study
the study label, for example “Silva 2019”


event.e
events in the experimental group


n.e
size of the experimental group


event.c
events in the control group


n.c
size of the control group



Any extra column is optional and becomes available later, for subgroup analysis and meta-regression. The example dataset carries Region, Design, RiskOfBias, MeanAge and FollowUpMonths.

title: Binary outcomes
text:
Step 2, the parameters

Summary measure (sm)
Default RR. It decides what gets pooled:

RR, risk ratio. The ratio of the event risks in the two groups.
OR, odds ratio. Needed if you will compare against literature that uses OR, or if you intend to use the Peto or GLMM methods, which only work with OR. Remember that the OR drifts away from the RR when the event is common.
RD, risk difference, on the absolute scale: the difference between the two event risks, read as events per 100 patients.



Method
Default inverse. It is the pooling method, and it exists only in this module and in single proportions:

inverse, inverse variance. The app default. Each study is weighted by the inverse of the variance of its effect estimate.
MH, Mantel-Haenszel. Uses the Mantel-Haenszel weights, computed from the cell counts rather than from the variance of the effect estimate.
Peto. Uses the one-step Peto odds ratio. Only works with sm = OR.
GLMM, generalized linear mixed model. Avoids the continuity corrections the other methods apply to zero cells. Slower. Only works with sm = OR, and the forest plot comes out without the Weight column, because a GLMM fit produces no per-study weight.







Peto and GLMM require OR



If you leave sm = RR or sm = RD and pick Peto or GLMM, the analysis stops with an error message. Switch sm to OR first, or set the method back to inverse or MH.




The other fields
Outcome name, the outcome direction and the group names work as described in Outcome settings.
Analysis model, Tau method, Random CI method and Prediction method work as described in Statistical settings (advanced). In this module the Prediction interval is off by default.

title: Binary outcomes
text:
Step 3, export and results
This module carries the full set of cards: forest plot, leave-one-out, funnel plot, small-study effects with Egger’s test, subgroup analysis, meta-regression and the two summary tables as XLSX. All of them are described in step 3 of the flow.

title: Continuous outcomes
text: Use this module when the outcome is a numeric measure: blood pressure, days in hospital, quality of life score. Follow the three-step flow; this page covers what the data has to look like and what changes in step 2.

title: Continuous outcomes
text:
Step 1, the data
Every study needs study, n.e and n.c. Then, for each group, whatever the paper actually reported.

Mean and standard deviation







Column
What it is




n.e, mean.e, sd.e
size, mean and SD of the experimental group


n.c, mean.c, sd.c
the same for the control group





A study reporting a median is accepted too







Column
What it is




n.e, median.e, q1.e, q3.e
size, median and quartiles of the experimental group


n.c, median.c, q1.c, q3.c
the same for the control group



min.e, max.e, min.c and max.c are optional. They can stand in for the quartiles when a paper reports only a range, and the conversion is then less precise.


The two can be mixed in one file
Fill the columns each study reports and leave the rest empty. The example dataset does exactly that: eight studies with mean and SD, four with median and quartiles. MetaVidence converts the median studies before pooling, using the method of Luo and colleagues for the mean and that of Shi and colleagues for the standard deviation, which are the current defaults of the meta package.
The Data check reports how many studies were converted, so the number is in front of you before anything runs and can go straight into the methods section.






The conversion has limits



It assumes an approximately symmetric distribution. With strongly skewed data, which is often exactly why the paper reported a median in the first place, the estimated mean may not represent the study well. Report how many studies were converted, and consider a sensitivity analysis without them.








A median with a standard deviation and nothing else



That pair cannot be converted, and MetaVidence refuses the file rather than accept it. Left alone, the meta package would drop those studies from the analysis without a word, and a meta-analysis that is quietly missing studies is worse than an error message.


The Data check otherwise works as in the binary module: it verifies the required columns, counts the studies, lists the columns left for subgroup and meta-regression and flags problems, including quartiles out of order.

title: Continuous outcomes
text:
Step 2, the parameters

Outcome settings
Outcome name, If the outcome increases, is that beneficial or harmful?, Experimental group name and Control group name work exactly as in the binary module.
Summary measure (sm) (default MD) decides the scale of the pooled result:

MD, mean difference. The result comes out in the original measurement unit, for example “3.2 fewer days in hospital”. It assumes every study used the same scale.
SMD, standardized mean difference. The result comes out in standard deviation units, with no measurement unit, so studies that used different instruments can be combined.



Statistical settings (advanced)
Analysis model, Tau method, Random CI method and Prediction method work exactly as in the flow.
Prediction interval here is on by default (Yes), unlike the binary module. Turn it off if you have fewer than 3 studies, or if the interval is so wide that it gets in the way of reading the figure.
There is no Method field in this module. Mantel-Haenszel, Peto and GLMM are methods for event counts, and do not apply to means.

title: Continuous outcomes
text:
Step 3, export and results
The cards are the same as in the binary module, with the same behavior:

Forest plot, with each study effect, the weights and the pooled diamond.
Leave-one-out analysis, to see whether a single study holds up the result.
Funnel plot and Small-study effects, the latter with Egger’s test.
Subgroup analysis, with the column selector inside the card itself.
Meta-regression, with numeric moderators and a bubble plot.
Subgroup summary table and Meta-regression summary table, as XLSX.







Check the sign before pooling



In continuous outcomes it is common for some studies to report change from baseline and others the final value. Mixing the two without thinking produces a meaningless pooled effect. Standardize before loading the spreadsheet.

title: The three-step flow
text:
Every MetaVidence module follows the same sequence, always in the same order: load the data, choose the parameters, review and export the results.
This page walks that whole flow, screen by screen. The images come from the binary outcomes module, but what is described here applies to all of them. Each module page covers only what changes in it.

title: The three-step flow
text:
The starting point

On the home page, click the card for the kind of data you have. The table on the tutorials home page says which module suits each format.

title: The three-step flow
text:
Step 1, the data

You have three routes, in the tabs of the card on the left:

Upload file takes an Excel or CSV file. The button to download the spreadsheet template sits next to it, already with the right column names.
Paste data pastes straight from Google Sheets or Excel.
Example loads 12 fictional studies, so you can explore the app without preparing anything.


The required columns
The collapsible guide just below the tabs lists what the spreadsheet needs, with the exact column names for that module. Each module page carries the same list.
Any extra column is optional. Text columns become available for subgroup analysis, numeric ones for meta-regression. The example datasets carry Region, Design, RiskOfBias, MeanAge and FollowUpMonths.


The data check

As soon as the data comes in, the Data check card reports back: whether all required columns are there, how many studies were detected, which columns are left for subgroup and meta-regression, and whether there are problems, such as blank cells, events larger than the total or sample sizes of zero.
It is worth reading before moving on. Fixing the spreadsheet now is faster than finding the error halfway through the analysis.
When everything checks out, click Next: parameters.

title: The three-step flow
text:
Step 2, the parameters

The fields come in two sections. Outcome settings opens by default, because it is the one you almost always touch. Statistical settings (advanced) starts collapsed, because the defaults suit most cases.
Every field has a “?” next to it carrying a summary of the explanation inside the app.

Outcome settings
Outcome name (default Outcome) goes into plot titles and exported file names. It is worth replacing with something short and specific, such as 30-day mortality, because that is how the file will reach your computer.
If the outcome increases, is that beneficial or harmful? (default Harmful) only sets the “Favors experimental” and “Favors control” labels under the forest plot. It changes no numbers. Choose Harmful for bad outcomes, such as death, and Beneficial for good ones, such as cure.
Experimental group name and Control group name set how the groups appear in the plots. Replacing them with real names, such as Anticoagulant and Placebo, leaves the figure ready for publication.
Summary measure (sm) decides what gets pooled, and the options change from module to module. It is the most important choice on this screen, so it is explained on each module page.
Single-arm has no direction and no group names, because there is no comparison. Network has two fields of its own here, and diagnostic accuracy has almost nothing. See the module page.


Statistical settings (advanced)
These fields are the same in most modules, with the same defaults.
Analysis model (default Random-effects).

Random-effects lets the true effect vary between studies.
Fixed-effect assumes every study estimates exactly the same effect.
Both draws the two lines on the same forest plot.

Tau method (default REML) is the estimator of the between-study variance, τ², which drives the random-effects weights, I² and the prediction interval. REML is restricted maximum likelihood, ML maximum likelihood, DL the DerSimonian-Laird estimator, and PM, SJ, HE, HS and EB the remaining estimators implemented in meta.
I-squared method (default Q) decides how I² is computed. Q uses the Higgins and Thompson definition, I² = (Q − df)/Q. From tau-squared derives it from the estimated τ² instead. The two answer different questions and can differ substantially on the same data: on the same four studies we get 89.9% with Q and 97.2% with τ².
Prediction interval adds the range where the effect of a future study is expected to fall. It needs at least 3 studies, and with 3 or 4 the interval comes out very wide. The default varies by module.
Random CI method (default classic) sets how the confidence interval of the pooled effect is computed under the random-effects model.

classic uses the normal approximation.
HK, Hartung-Knapp, uses the t distribution, which usually widens the interval.
KR, Kenward-Roger, follows the same idea with a variance adjustment.

Prediction method (default V) sets how the prediction interval is computed. V uses the t distribution with k-1 degrees of freedom and HTS uses t with k-2.
Method, the pooling method, exists only in the binary and single-proportion modules, with different options in each. See the module page.


Subgroup and meta-regression
These two columns are not chosen here. In single-outcome analysis and in batch mode alike, you pick them in step 3, inside the result card itself, and the analysis is re-run for the column you choose.
When you are ready, click Run analysis.

title: The three-step flow
text:
Step 3, export and results

The 3. Results and citation card at the top carries the analysis status and the citation reminder. Below it comes the results grid.
Each result has its own card. Most carry Preview to see it on screen, Summary for the numeric output and Download to save. A few cards have no preview, and there the button reads Download plot so it cannot be mistaken for the summary. Format, width and height sit in each card: PNG exports at 600 DPI and PDF exports as vector, both suitable for submission.






Plot came out clipped?



Increase the height on the card itself and download again. That fixes almost every clipping case, because the plot area is shared between the study rows and the footer with the statistics.








Download before you leave



Do not reload or close the tab while you still have a result you have not downloaded. The app keeps everything in the memory of the session: reloading starts a new one, and the loaded data and the results are gone. There is no way to get them back without running the analysis again.


Not every module carries all the cards below. Network and diagnostic accuracy have sets of their own, described on their pages.

Forest plot

The main plot. Each study with its effect and confidence interval, the weight it received, and the diamond of the pooled effect at the bottom. Below it come the heterogeneity statistics (τ², Q, I²) and the test of the overall effect.


Leave-one-out analysis
Redoes the pooling dropping one study at a time, and plots the result of each round. It answers whether a single study is holding up the conclusion. If the estimate barely moves, the result is robust. If one study flips the direction or the significance, that belongs in the paper.


Funnel plot
The funnel plot, effect against precision. Asymmetry suggests publication bias, but it can also come from real heterogeneity or from small studies of differing quality. Interpret with caution below 10 studies.


Small-study effects
This card has only the Summary button, and it opens the Egger test result with an interpretation note. It is the formal test for the asymmetry you saw in the funnel.


Subgroup analysis

Pick a column in the selector inside the card and the plot is redrawn immediately. There is no need to go back to step 2 or rerun the analysis.
The overall pooled effect does not change when you ask for subgroups. The same analysis is rerun with the same parameters, only partitioned. What you gain is the effect within each level and the test for subgroup differences at the bottom.


Meta-regression
Pick a numeric moderator and the app draws the bubble plot, with each bubble sized by the study weight, and the fitted line. Summary gives the coefficient, the interval, the p value and the model R².
The selector lists numeric columns only, such as MeanAge or FollowUpMonths. Categorical moderators belong in the subgroup analysis, not in this card.






Meta-regression needs studies



A common rule of thumb is at least 10 studies per moderator. Below that the coefficient is unstable and the line looks more convincing than it is.




Subgroup summary table and Meta-regression summary table
Here you select several columns at once and get a single table. The subgroup one gives the effect per level, the number of studies, I² and the interaction p value for each variable. The meta-regression one gives the coefficients of each numeric moderator. These are the tables that usually go into the paper, and both export as XLSX.

title: How to cite
How to cite
How to cite
text:
Cite the analysis packages too
MetaVidence does not do the maths itself. It calls meta, metafor, netmeta and mada, and those packages implement the models. Cite the ones your analysis used, and record each version.
In R, citation("meta") gives the exact wording for each. Which ones apply depends on the module:







Module
Packages behind it




Binary, continuous, pre-calculated, single-arm
meta, and metafor for meta-regression


Network meta-analysis
netmeta


Diagnostic test accuracy
mada, and meta for the forest plots

title: Multiple outcomes at once
text:
Follow the steps on this page to analyse mortality, recurrence and adverse events in a single run, and download each kind of plot with every outcome already inside one ZIP.
It works in these modules: binary outcomes, continuous outcomes, the three pre-calculated ones, single proportions and single means. Network and diagnostic accuracy do not have this mode.

title: Multiple outcomes at once
text:
1. Download the template

Open the module you are going to use.
In the Data step, go to the card on the right, More than one outcome.
Click Download XLSX template, next to the file field.

You get a workbook with three sheets already filled in and in the right format. Start from that file, not from the template in the left card, which is for a single outcome and has a different structure.

title: Multiple outcomes at once
text:
2. Build your workbook
Open the template and follow these rules:

Keep one sheet per outcome. Add or delete sheets until you have as many as you have outcomes.
Rename each sheet with the outcome name. Write 30-day mortality, not Sheet1. That name goes into the plot titles and into the exported file names.
Fill each sheet as if it were a separate analysis. Every study for that outcome, with every required column of the module.
Use the same column names in every sheet, exactly as they appear in the template.
Repeat a study in as many sheets as it belongs to. Sheets do not talk to each other: no study is linked to its counterpart in another sheet.
Save as .xlsx.







Sheet name rules



Excel caps sheet names at 31 characters and rejects : \ / ? * [ ]. When generating files, MetaVidence replaces anything that is not a letter or a digit with _, so Progression-free survival reaches your computer as Progression_free_survival.








Going to use subgroups or meta-regression?



Include the column in every sheet where you want that result. If it is missing from one sheet, that outcome runs without the subgroup and the app records why, instead of stopping the whole run.

title: Multiple outcomes at once
text:
3. Upload the workbook

Go back to the More than one outcome card.
Click Browse under Import multi-outcome workbook (.xlsx).
Pick your file.

Do not use the field in the left card. It reads only the first sheet and treats the file as a single outcome.

title: Multiple outcomes at once
text:
4. Check the Data check
The Data check card now shows one row per outcome, with the number of studies found in each.
Read it before moving on. If a sheet has a missing column or an invalid value, fix the workbook and upload again. That is faster than finding the error after running everything.

title: Multiple outcomes at once
text:
5. Set the parameters
Click Next: parameters. One thing changes on this screen in batch mode: the Outcome name field disappears, because the sheet name now names each outcome.
Choose the sm, the model and the rest as usual. One single set of parameters applies to every outcome. Subgroup and meta-regression are not set here: you pick those columns in step 3, inside the result card, exactly as in single-outcome mode.






One sm for all



If one outcome needs RR and another needs MD, do not put both in the same file. Split them into two workbooks and do two runs.

title: Multiple outcomes at once
text:
6. Run the analysis
Click Run analysis. The app processes each sheet, one at a time, and moves on to step 3.

title: Multiple outcomes at once
text:
7. Download the results
In batch mode each result card gains an extra button. For every plot you want:

Click 1. Run analysis, inside the card.
Wait for the button beside it to stop showing 2. Download locked.
Click 2. Download.

The Subgroup analysis and Meta-regression cards also carry a column picker. Pick the column there, then click 1. Run analysis in that same card. Changing the column locks the download again, so click 1. Run analysis once more to rebuild the files for the new column.
Choose the format, the width and the height before downloading, in the fields of that card. They apply to every outcome in that ZIP.
You get a file named Forest_Batch.zip, and inside it one plot per outcome, with the sheet name in the file name. Repeat for the funnel, the leave-one-out and whatever else you need.






Prepare only what you will use



Each click on 1. Run analysis draws that plot for every outcome. With many outcomes that takes time, so prepare only the cards that go into the paper.

title: Pre-calculated effects
text:
Use this module when you extracted the already calculated effect from the papers, rather than the raw counts. That is the typical case for hazard ratios (HR) from survival analyses, which rarely come with enough data to recompute.
Follow the three-step flow. Here I cover the three input formats and the field that decides whether your analysis comes out right.

title: Pre-calculated effects
text:
Step 1, the data
There are three submodules, chosen on the previous page. Pick the one that matches what you managed to extract from the papers.



Format
Required columns
Needs a standard error?




TE with 95% CI
study, TE, lower, upper
no


TE with standard error
study, TE, seTE
yes


Full set
study, TE, seTE, lower, upper
yes



n.e and n.c are optional in all three formats and appear in the forest plot when present. Any other column stays available for subgroup analysis and meta-regression.






What each format asks for



TE with 95% CI is the only one where you type no standard error at all: the app derives it from the interval. The other two ask for seTE directly.


The Data check verifies the columns, counts the studies and validates the interval, requiring lower <= TE <= upper. If you swapped two columns, it warns you here, before the analysis runs.

title: Pre-calculated effects
text:
Step 2, the parameters

Outcome settings
Outcome name, If the outcome increases, is that beneficial or harmful?, Experimental group name and Control group name work as in the binary module.
Summary measure (sm) (default HR) offers six options, and here it does more than label the axis: it decides whether your numbers go through a log transformation.

Ratio measures: HR, RR, OR. Pooling happens on the log scale and the result returns to the original scale in the plots.
Difference measures: RD, MD, SMD. No transformation.



The scale of TE
This is where mistakes happen most, and it is worth reading carefully.
For ratio measures, MetaVidence expects the value as reported in the paper, not the logarithm. If the paper says “HR 0.76 (95% CI 0.61 to 0.95)”, you type 0.76, 0.61 and 0.95. Typing the logarithm makes the app reject the spreadsheet, since it requires positive values for ratio measures.
For difference measures, the value is already on the right scale and nothing is transformed.






Check sm before running



The sm chosen in Outcome settings decides whether your numbers go through the log transformation. Choosing MD when the data are ratios, or the other way round, produces a result that looks plausible and is wrong. It is the kind of error no validation catches, because every number is valid.








Careful: seTE goes on a different scale from TE



For ratio measures the two fields do not share a scale. TE goes in as reported, 0.76. seTE goes in on the log scale, which is how papers report it and how the calculation uses it. For the example above, seTE would be 0.113, not 0.087.
Getting this wrong raises no error at all: you get a plausible confidence interval that is wrong. The way to avoid the decision altogether is the TE with 95% CI format, which needs no seTE.




Statistical settings (advanced)
Analysis model, Tau method, Random CI method and Prediction method work exactly as in the flow.
Prediction interval is off by default (No) in all three submodules.
There is no Method field: the effect already comes calculated, so pooling is always by inverse variance.

title: Pre-calculated effects
text:
Step 3, export and results
Every card from the binary module is here, with the same behavior: Forest plot, Leave-one-out analysis, Funnel plot, Small-study effects with Egger’s test, Subgroup analysis and Meta-regression, plus the two summary tables as XLSX.
